note.label: TABERNACLES THE GOODLY BOUGHS

precepts.text: Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt; she sent out her boughs unto the sea.
precepts.point: His boughs, Israel, were delivered to death in the nether parts of the earth, and the nations shook at his fall.

note.label: The Kingdom Of Adam And The Old World

precepts.why:
Pharaoh is asked who he is like in his greatness, and the answer is the great cedar: “Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches.” The Lord speaks to the prophets by similitudes, saying one thing that means another, and here he compares the Egyptian kingdom to Adam's kingdom, Adam ruling, to give us more insight into what we read in Genesis. “The waters made him great”: the waters that came from the Father made Adam great, flowing from him through all his plants, all Adam's children. And “his boughs were multiplied.” What are the boughs that multiplied?

Asaph answers in Psalm 80, crying to the “Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a flock”: “Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it. Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land. The hills were covered with the shadow of it, and the boughs thereof were like the goodly cedars. She sent out her boughs unto the sea, and her branches unto the river.”

Those boughs are Israel, the sons of God. All of this is talking about Israel: all of us that were drinking that water, and everybody was not getting that water like us. Isaiah says the same: “In that day shall the branch of the Lord be beautiful and glorious.” The branches of the Lord are Israel, those of us that escape the destruction and get the kingdom.

So the boughs multiplied on the great cedar are Adam's true children, Israel, and the same vine the Lord brought out of Egypt and planted is the vine that filled the land with its shadow in Adam's kingdom.

precepts.text: Under the goodly cedar shall dwell all fowl of every wing.
precepts.point: His boughs, Israel, were delivered to death in the nether parts of the earth, and the nations shook at his fall.

note.label: The Kingdom Of Adam And The Old World

precepts.why:
Ezekiel 31 says the great cedar was “of an high stature”, and “All the fowls of heaven made their nests in his boughs.” The fowls of heaven are the angels: all the angels were under Adam when he was ruling, as it says, “let all the angels of God worship him.” Under his branches the beasts of the field brought forth their young, and the serpent was “more subtil than any beast of the field”: Satan was there, under Adam. And “under his shadow dwelt all great nations”, all the nations of the earth.

Ezekiel 17 shows the same cedar planted again: “I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent.” That is talking about Christ. “In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell.” That is the same as Ezekiel 31. He will plant it in the height of Israel, where it was before.

“And all the trees of the field shall know that I the Lord have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish.” He brought us down, and he raises us back up again. Ezra saw it too: on mount Sion, in the midst of a great people, “a young man of a high stature, taller than all the rest.”

To understand the kingdom of Adam you have to understand the kingdom that is to come. It will be the same thing: us ruling with Christ in righteousness, with all the fowl dwelling under the goodly cedar, and nobody able to hurt us.

precepts.text: Through envy of the devil came death into the world.
precepts.point: His boughs, Israel, were delivered to death in the nether parts of the earth, and the nations shook at his fall.

note.label: The Kingdom Of Adam And The Old World

precepts.why:
The great cedar was so fair that “all the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God, envied him.” The fir trees were not like his boughs, the chesnut trees not like his branches. His boughs and branches were his true children, his firstborn in the heavens, immortal and ruling with him. The other trees were the children Adam had on the earth before the fall, not created in his image, the multitude “born in vain.” They envied him, and they envied the twelve tribes that were with him.

Wisdom of Solomon shows who else envied him: “For God created man to be immortal, and made him to be an image of his own eternity. Nevertheless through envy of the devil came death into the world.” The man God created was Adam. Adam was immortal and his sons were immortal; the children he had on the earth were created as men, sons of men, and were not immortal.

The devil also envied Adam. Satan went to war with Adam, and when he could not get him, he went through his woman to take him down: he jumped on his wife, played with her emotions and tricked her. Through the envy of Satan, that is how death came.

It will be the same in the future: “The heathen shall envy thee, but they shall be able to do nothing against thee.” When Christ returns and sets us back on this earth to rule, the nations will envy us, the same as back then, but they will not be able to do anything against us.

precepts.text: They are all delivered unto death, to the nether parts of the earth.
precepts.point: His boughs, Israel, were delivered to death in the nether parts of the earth, and the nations shook at his fall.

note.label: The Kingdom Of Adam And The Old World

precepts.why:
The great cedar that was lifted up in his height was driven out “for his wickedness”, and the Lord gives the end of it: “To the end that none of all the trees by the waters exalt themselves for their height, neither shoot up their top among the thick boughs, neither their trees stand up in their height, all that drink water: for they are all delivered unto death, to the nether parts of the earth, in the midst of the children of men, with them that go down to the pit.”

We are all delivered unto death. All that drank the water, his boughs, his branches, Israel, now have to come down on the earth and die as men. Before that we had our spiritual body, our angelic body. They go down “in the midst of the children of men” because they were not regular men. That goes back to “I have said, Ye are gods”, and “ye shall die like men.”

Read on: “In the day when he went down to the grave I caused a mourning: I covered the deep for him, and I restrained the floods thereof, and the great waters were stayed.” The day Adam was cast out, the waters his boughs and branches were drinking were restrained. No water was coming to Adam anymore. Those great waters are the same living waters of Revelation 22; they stopped when Adam fell. Lebanon mourned for him and all the trees of the field fainted for him: his children.

“I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to hell.” Hell there is the grave, the earth. When Adam fell, the Lord withdrew paradise, a spiritual realm connected to the earth, and it caused devastation, and millions died, as Ezra says, “as death was to Adam, so was the flood to these.” That is where Cain found his wife: not everybody died.

And “all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon”, Adam's top leaders, “shall be comforted in the nether parts of the earth.” We are comforted here by the scriptures, “that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.”

precepts.text: The tree planted by the rivers of water is the man whose delight is in the law of the Lord, so the water is God's laws, his commandments, his wisdom.
precepts.point: No tree in the garden of God was like him, and all the trees of Eden envied him, because Adam was the one to go to and he ruled everything.

precepts.text: The trees in the garden of God are men among whom a man may seek to hide.
precepts.point: The trees of the garden here are people. Adam and his wife tried to hide their sins among the other people that were in the garden with them.

note.label: Genesis 3: The Craftiness of Your Enemy

precepts.why:
“The cedars in the garden of God could not hide him: the fir trees were not like his boughs, and the chesnut trees were not like his branches; nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty.” The trees in the garden of God are men, and a man may seek to hide among them.

That is what Adam and his wife did. The trees of the garden here are people, and when they “hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the garden”, they were trying to hide their sins among the other people that were in the garden with them.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

precepts.why:
“For the first Adam bearing a wicked heart transgressed”: the first Adam, because there were other Adams after him. “Bearing a wicked heart”: in Genesis 3 he didn’t know he was naked, or had a wicked heart, until they actually performed wickedness; then they realized at that moment that they were naked. He “was overcome”, by Eve, “and so be all they that are born of him”: they have a wicked heart and can be overcome.

“Thus infirmity was made permanent”: sin was made permanent through Adam. Out of Adam’s loins you are sinful. “And the law (also) in the heart of the people with the malignity of the root”: the law was put in us, but there was also the good and evil in us. You have the old man in you and the new man there, an ongoing battle in us from the moment we’re born. Adam learned good and evil, so anything that came out of him had good and evil inside of it. That’s the root.

Malignant means tending to produce death or deterioration: it corrupts over time. It’s cancerous, it’s bad. When Adam did what he did, his seed that came out of him was bound to deteriorate. Did he die immediately when he got kicked out? No. Satan told Eve, ye shall not surely die: not immediately, but over time you and your descendants will deteriorate.

“So that the good departed away”: the law in time was forgotten, because Adam died and the law was dismissed after a while, “and the evil abode still”: the evil spread.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

precepts.why:
“Unto him thou gavest commandment to love thy way: which he transgressed, and immediately thou appointedst death in him”. Remember Satan said, ye shall not surely die; this says that as soon as he went in with Eve, immediately. Death came to him immediately, but he died over time: deterioration, malignity. “And in his generations, of whom came nations, tribes, people, and kindreds, out of number”: out of Eve.

“And every people walked after their own will”: at the fall of Adam, “and did wonderful things before thee”, meaning evil stuff before God, “and despised thy commandments”, because the law was with us at first, but then the evil abode still and the law was forgotten.

“And again in process of time”: keep those three words in mind. Process of time means a while; it could be a hundred years later. “Thou broughtest the flood upon those that dwelt in the world, and destroyedst them. And it came to pass in every of them, that as death was to Adam, so was the flood to these.” When Adam died it was as catastrophic as the flood was. That’s why Ezekiel 31 says that at his fall the nations shook. It wasn’t, okay Adam, get out, time to go, and everyone just walked out. It was very, very bad.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

precepts.why:
All this had to happen to bring us to Christ. It was all predestined to happen: the Lord’s plan, his screenplay, and we’re all just actors in it. “For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly”: he didn’t want to be, “but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope”.

He made Adam sinful on purpose. He knew Adam would fall into that, so that it would bring sin into the world, so that Christ would come into the world and grant us repentance and grant us life. The Father knew this. That was God’s plan from the very beginning.

points: “Son of man, speak unto Pharaoh king of Egypt, and to his multitude”: his army, his realm. “Whom art thou like in thy greatness?” Who do you resemble, Pharaoh, in your greatness, before you fall? This chapter is a parable, a comparison between Pharaoh in his greatness and someone else.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with fair branches”: a cedar is a tree in Lebanon. He mentions the Assyrian because the Assyrians conquered Egypt; before Assyria came into power, Pharaoh, Egypt, was in its greatness. “His top was among the thick boughs”: powerful.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “The waters made him great”, and his height was exalted above all the trees of the field “because of the multitude of waters”. It’s talking about somebody else here, and it’s going to elaborate.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “Under his shadow dwelt all great nations.” Remember Ezra said that out of Adam came kindreds, people, tribes and nations.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “Thus was he fair in his greatness, in the length of his branches: for his root was by great waters”: meaning great wisdom came from him.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “The cedars in the garden of God could not hide him”: the cedars in the garden of God, in paradise, could not hide him, because he stood out from all the rest. He was the most glorified of them all. “Nor any tree in the garden of God was like unto him in his beauty”: because he was the wisest.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “All the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God, envied him.” How can a tree envy? A tree is not a person. The tree is not a tree, it’s a person: people are trees, because trees are abundant and very tall, huge.

So it’s talking about Adam here. Adam is being compared to both Assyria and Pharaoh, because Assyria was a very ancient empire that reigned in the beginning, and Egypt was a very ancient empire that reigned in the beginning.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “Because thou hast lifted up thyself in height”: “I have therefore delivered him into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen”, Egypt falling into Assyria. “I have driven him out for his wickedness”: who was driven out for wickedness? Adam. It goes back and forth between them.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “And strangers, the terrible of the nations, have cut him off”: going into Assyria and Egypt. “His branches are fallen, and his boughs are broken”: when Adam fell, all the wisdom Adam taught the people began to diminish; it’s gone, Adam is gone. “And all the people of the earth are gone down from his shadow”: from Adam’s shadow. And they left him, “Upon his ruin”.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “To the end that none of all the trees by the waters exalt themselves for their height”: because their understanding starts to diminish, and they lose their stature over time. “For they are all delivered unto death”: when Adam died, Ezra says death was appointed in him and in his generations.

“To the nether parts of the earth”: nether means lower in position, lying beneath the earth’s surface, infernal, lower or under. Adam was in paradise before, and he was brought to the nether part: Adam got kicked out and he got put here. This is nether earth we’re in now. This is garbage, the bottom. That’s why he told Satan, you’re going to rule this. All the nations that are beneath us remain here. “In the midst of the children of men”: everybody else, “with them that go down to the pit”, with them that die.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “In the day when he went down to the grave”: when Adam died, “I caused a mourning”. Everyone cried: this dude died, and now we’re all going to die with him. We had paradise, now we’re going to be on earth. When Adam got kicked out, everyone got kicked out, the tribes, the nations, the people. God said, all of you get out, because you’re all like him. Now we can’t grow no more, we’re going to lose our stature, we’re getting dumber, because Adam is gone.

“I covered the deep for him”: all the deep understanding and wisdom they had through Adam, they’re losing it now he’s gone. “And all the trees of the field fainted for him”: trees don’t faint, people do. The trees fainted for Adam when he died, meaning his children.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to hell with them that descend into the pit”. When Adam fell it was catastrophic. Whatever it was, they don’t say, but it was bad, very bad. “All the trees of Eden”, “all that drink water, shall be comforted in the nether parts of the earth”: comforted here.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “They also went down into hell with him”: everyone got kicked out, everyone is on nether earth now. “Unto them that be slain with the sword”: death was appointed in them too, like him. “They that were his arm, that dwelt under his shadow in the midst of the heathen”: his arm is his flesh, his descendants.

note.label: Good And Evil | Generation To Generation: From Beginning To End

points: “To whom art thou thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden?” He asks the question again. Pharaoh, before Assyria conquered you, you were like Adam: boastful, people came under you for sanctuary, you had resources, wealth, power, everybody came to you to learn wisdom. Now where are you? Assyria came and destroyed you. Adam was like both of them in a certain way: like Assyria in his glory and like Pharaoh in glory, but both their falls were terrible and everybody felt it, the same way everyone felt it when Adam fell.

“Yet shalt thou be brought down with the trees of Eden unto the nether parts of the earth”, with everybody else. “This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, saith the Lord God”: but it’s not just Pharaoh, it’s who he’s compared to also. Pharaoh and Adam.
